Council of Ministers: review of Boni Yayi's 10 years

The Council of Ministers met in extraordinary session on Tuesday 29 March 2016, chaired by the President of the Republic, Head of State, Head of Government.

At the beginning of the session, the Head of State observed a minute of silence in memory of the late:

- Natiwan David Taman, father-in-law of Mr Thomas Tchoropa Yombo, Minister in charge of Relations with Institutions;
- Helene Ayaba Houede, mother-in-law of Inspector General of Brigade Theophile N'dah, retired;
- Rene Akanzan Tindo, paternal grandfather of Mr Ernest Ayivi Tindo, Deputy Director General of the National Council of Shippers of Benin.

The Council of Ministers was largely devoted to the summarised points of the government's achievements in the ministries since 2006. The achievements may be followed in detail on the government's website: www.gouv.bj.

I - Thus in the field of the economy,

of finance and of denationalisation programmes, the macroeconomic framework remained broadly stable over the period 2006-2015. It was characterised by rapid economic growth, contained inflation, a controlled public deficit and efforts to consolidate and modernise public finances.

Over the period 2006-2015, the economic growth rate stood on average at 4.2%, with a sustained level over the last three years (6.0% on average) and a peak of about 7.0% in 2013. The acceleration of economic growth over the last ten (10) years is attributable in particular to:

- The acceleration of port reforms: creation of a one-stop shop for formalities at the Port of Cotonou, construction and concessioning of a new quay, strengthening of security, etc.;
- the programme of reforms at the level of the agricultural sector, which made it possible to increase agricultural production. Cotton production rose from 191,000 tonnes in 2005 to 393,000 tonnes in 2014, an increase of 105.8%;
- The densification of the productive fabric with the establishment of new industrial production units (for example Nocibe);
- the implementation of a policy of major public works (improvement of the road network and modernisation of the large cities);
- the consolidation of public finances and the strengthening of the macroeconomic framework, etc.

On average over the last ten (10) years, the inflation rate was kept at 2.7%, below the average of 3.0 prescribed by WAEMU (Uemoa).

At the level of public finances, State revenue rose from 383.4 billion CFA francs in 2005 to 819.5 billion CFA francs in 2015, an increase of 113.7%. The tax burden rate rose from 13.2% in 2005 to 15.0% on average over the last ten (10) years. This progression shows the government's efforts to strengthen the mobilisation of tax resources.

As regards expenditure, it came to 1,242.3 billion CFA francs in 2015, thus exceeding for the first time the symbolic threshold of 1,000 billion CFA francs, compared with 494 billion CFA francs in 2005. This resulted in an increase of more than 150%.

The growth of expenditure is driven by investment spending and by the wage bill.

Investment expenditure grew by 161% over the last ten years, rising from 144.2 billion CFA francs in 2005 to 376.9 billion CFA francs in 2015. As regards the investment rate, it would stand at 29% according to the BCEAO figures, compared with 16.5% in 2005.

As regards the wage bill, it recorded a jump of 155% over the period. As a percentage of tax revenue, a WAEMU convergence criterion, the ratio stood at 48.2% in 2015 compared with 35.6% in 2006, a jump of more than 10 percentage points, in connection with the various benefits granted to civil servants.

Faced with this increase in revenue, the budget deficit stood on average at around 3.9% of GDP compared with 4.4% in 2005.

It should also be stressed that the various reforms implemented have made it possible to strengthen budgetary transparency. Thus, the budget transparency index rose from 1/100 in 2012 to 45/100 in 2015, moving Benin up from last position to second place within WAEMU, just after Mali.

Benin's public debt is sustainable, with a debt ratio of about 41.7% at the end of December 2015, against a community ceiling of 70%. This management of public debt is supported by a prudent borrowing strategy, annexed to the Finance Act. Thus the domestic debt relating to expenditure on the acquisition of goods and services by the public administration is valued at 161,572,038,464 CFA francs, broken down as follows:

- pending authorisation at the Directorate General of the Budget: 79,796,912,683 CFA francs
- pending payment at the Directorate General of the Budget and Public Accounting (DGTCP): 81,775,125,781 CFA francs

With regard to the public debt comprising the external debt and the domestic debt managed by the Autonomous Sinking Fund (Caa), it is valued at 2,080,533,220,500 CFA francs, of which 1,036,946,793,060 CFA francs in respect of the outstanding domestic debt and 1,043,586,427,44 CFA francs for the outstanding external debt.

Exports of goods [rose] from 304.9 billion CFA francs in 2005 to 1,061.4 billion CFA francs in 2014 and 1,111.9 billion CFA francs expected for 2015, that is more than a tripling in the space of 10 years. As regards imports, they rose from 456.6 billion CFA francs in 2005 to 1,532.9 billion CFA francs in 2015, driven among other things by imports of food products and capital goods.

Benin was ranked, for two consecutive years, in the top 10 of the best reforming countries in the world.

During the year 2014 Benin benefited from an amount of incoming foreign direct investment (FDI) of $377 million, that is about 226 billion CFA francs, according to the 2015 World Investment Report of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), published on 24 June 2015.

The Beninese economy thus absorbed in 2014 more than 7 times the amount of foreign capital of 2006, which was $53 million, that is an increase of more than 600% over the said period.

The sectors that mainly benefited from these foreign financial capital flows in Benin are Tourism/Hotels, Industry, Construction and Public Works, Energy, mining (petroleum), etc.

These new UNCTAD data today make the Beninese economy the 3rd most attractive economy of WAEMU for foreign capital and the 8th in West Africa, whereas it represented the 6th destination of WAEMU and the 13th in West Africa in 2006.

In the field of Public Works and Transport, the review of achievements presented by the Minister of State in charge of Public Works and Transport shows that the road network evolved from a length of 1,821 km in 2006 to about 2,800 km in 2016, that is an increase of 1,000 km for an investment of more than 850 billion CFA francs, corresponding on average to 100 km per year in terms of rehabilitation, modernisation and extension.

As part of the extension and modernisation of Benin's road infrastructure, the Government has initiated a programme of about 2,000 km of roads spread over the entire national territory. The financing of this programme is provided by the national budget in its study phase and by loans contracted directly by the companies on behalf of the State. These road projects under this innovative financing arrangement concern more than 1,850 km of roads for an amount of more than 1,418 billion CFA francs.

The review of achievements in the public works and transport sector also covered road safety and rail and air transport.

In the field of energy - Challenges

Energy balance: 48.3% hydrocarbons, 3% electricity, 49.5% traditional biomass. An energy revolution is needed to achieve an emerging Benin.

National electricity production portfolio: thermal power plants out of order and rented generating sets that are not very efficient (225 CFA francs/kWh). The average electrification rate is 20%, with only 5.5% in rural areas.

Structural deficit between production capacity and demand, coupled with the fragility and obsolescence of our distribution network.

No tool for network management and analysis.

The narrowness of our domestic market, the small size of our electricity system and the absence of an attractive legal framework represent an almost insurmountable barrier to private investment.

The provisions of the public procurement code represent a major barrier to the performance of this essential service.

The large State subsidies, often poorly targeted, have not made it possible to stem debts of more than twenty billion CFA francs owed to the Electricity Community of Benin and to TCN of Nigeria.

The deficiencies in the management of SBEE's customer base, with enormous delays in the recovery of receivables, lead to a cash position incapable of meeting electricity purchase contracts and any investment of its own.

Means

- signature in September 2015 of the second MCC Compact for 403 million USD devoted exclusively to the electric power sector.
- Adoption of a National Emergency Energy Programme (PEUN).
- Establishment of a coordination and monitoring unit.

Signature of concession agreements and electricity purchase contracts with seven (7) developers, namely:

- putting in place bank payment guarantees acceptable to investors.
- Compared with the tendering process started almost 12 months ago now for the project to build at Maria-Gleta a 120 MW dual-fuel power plant financed by the IsDB/BOAD/EBID, we are still 6 to 8 months away from the choice of a supplier and the start of works.

For the hydroelectric power plants we have achieved two major objectives:

Official launch on 26 December 2015, on the Mono river, of the works of the Adjarala Hydroelectric Power Plant (147 MW).

On the Oueme river, negotiations with Sinohydro for the development of the whole hydroelectric basin of the Oueme river with Chinese financing, beginning with Dogo Bis for 128 MW and followed by Beterou and Vossa. Under the memorandum of understanding, Sinohydro will finance:

- all the feasibility and environmental studies,
- the creation in Benin of a Centre of Excellence for the maintenance and upkeep of all these thermal and hydroelectric power plants in West Africa,
- the computerisation of all the central directorates of the ministry.

1 - For the Strengthening of the Electricity Network and Rural Electrification, the flagship actions concerned:

- The carrying out of works to install protection and measurement equipment in the substations in order to ensure loop operation of the CEB southern network; (ii) the continuation of the works to build a 161 kV electrical interconnection line of 280 km between Onigbolo and Parakou and a 161 kV electrical interconnection line between Sakete and Porto-Novo; (iii) the start of the works to build the Kandi-Banikoara medium-voltage line;
- the completion of the rural electrification works of the energy facility project in the 105 localities, followed by the project of the 66 localities;
- with financing from AFD, the EIB and the EU, the project to restructure and extend the SBEE networks in the commune of Abomey-Calavi and the department of the Atlantique is at the stage of selecting a consultant and finalising the various execution tender documents.

The ongoing execution of the project of the 67 localities with Indian financing, with factory acceptance testing now completed.

The ongoing execution of the project of the 17 localities financed by the national budget.

In total we have:

- Built 2,570 km of medium-voltage line and 1,527 km of low-voltage line
- 31,272 distribution transformers
- Facilitated access to electricity for nearly one million people.
- 50% of our 3,762 localities are electrified.

The prepaid meter programme concerned World Bank financing for the acquisition and installation of 45,000 meters. In addition, the Council of Ministers authorised the acquisition and installation of 35,000 meters.

The programmes of the solar photovoltaic sector concern:

- financing by the national budget (loan through the BOAD) with ANADER as contracting authority and SABER as delegated contracting authority for the solar energy development programme (Proves). The acquisition and installation of the following was launched:
  - 15,000 solar street lamps throughout the national territory;
  - 105 solar micro-power plants with low-voltage networks in 105 localities not crossed by the SBEE network throughout the national territory;
  - 105 solar pumping systems with water towers;
- financing by the national budget with ANADER as contracting authority, the programme of 1,500 solar street lamps, of 200 solar kits of 1,000 W and of 2,000 kits of 7 W throughout the national territory;
- financing by the Council of the Entente with ANADER as contracting authority, the project of 400 solar kits of 7 W distributed in Djegbadji (Ouidah), Koute (Segbana) and Djigbewo (Ze);
- financing by the national budget and several Technical and Financial Partners of the "Light for All" programme.

4 - The master plan: under the leadership of the Directorate General of Energy, a national committee made up of technicians and senior officials was tasked with using the results of the work of the IED consultancy firm and the orientations of the PEUN to produce a master plan for the sector.

The validation workshop will be held during the third quarter of 2016.

5 - The special projects financed by AFD concern:

After several working sessions and expert missions, AFD has accepted in principle to finance three projects:

- The installation of computerised management equipment (DMS = Distribution Management System)
- The computerisation of SBEE's customer management, which will allow greater transparency, more efficiency and reliability in the company's customer management
- The contribution to the construction of one or more solar power plants with a total capacity of 20 MW with attractive tariffs per kWh.

10. Project to grant a concession for the 80 MW gas turbine power plant at Maria-Gleta

Authorisation was obtained from the Council of Ministers to proceed with the concessioning of the 80 MW gas turbine power plant at Maria-Gleta. Steps have been initiated with the DNCMP to obtain authorisation to launch a restricted tender.

The terms of reference are prepared for the choice of a consultancy firm to carry out the audit of the plant and establish its technical and financial valuation. The majority of the technical documents required to launch the tenders are also available.

Concerning the restoration of the financial equilibrium of the electricity sector, it is proposed to submit for the approval of the Council of Ministers a project that takes into account the elements below:

- Putting in place methods and procedures for mastering the Financial Model faithfully representing the organisation and the costs of SBEE's activities and services.
- Definition of a tariff policy adjusted according to consumers' ability to pay and the government's socio-political objectives
- Determination of the amount of the State subsidy to compensate for the gap between SBEE's costs and revenues
- Putting in place procedures and resources for the recovery of receivables and revenues (the prepayment principle is applied to the government and to State enterprises)
- Estimation of the annual investment needs for the implementation of the master plan,
- Putting in place mechanisms for financing investments in the energy sector.

Conclusions and recommendations

With the effective implementation of the construction of the power plants under the signed power purchase agreements, the period of national emergency for increasing production capacity is no longer to be invoked. New additions of production capacity must now be subject to competitive tendering procedures. It is thus recommended to:

Continue the planning and execution of the main lines of the National Emergency Energy Programme (PEUN). In particular, the human and material resources and the determination necessary for the following must be mobilised:

- the restructuring of the sector's companies and agencies;
- the restructuring of the ministry and mainly of the directorates general of energy and hydrocarbons;
- the formalisation and adoption of an Electricity Code that is modern and able to meet the current challenges of the sector and the regulatory role of the ARE;
- the ratification of the Benin-Togo Electricity Code;
- the definition and execution of the Programme to restore the financial equilibrium of the electricity sector;
- the finalisation and execution of the master plan;
- the establishment of the energy sector financing fund;
- put in place a mechanism and governance to strengthen coordination between the MERPMDER and the MCC;
- prepare and hold the next review of the sector, which must take stock of ongoing projects, present and explain the PEUN, present the MCC programme, determine the convergences between the PEUN and the MCC, present the master plan, present the plan and timetable of reforms and propose monitoring and coordination mechanisms within the ministry and with the Technical and Financial Partners;
- Finally, a strategy and an action plan must be developed to give concrete form to the commitments and benefits of COP21, making the best use of all the international programmes for access to sustainable energy for African countries.

Furthermore, in order to promote access to energy for populations far from SBEE's conventional network, Benin has developed renewable energy projects and programmes. In this respect, four projects/programmes have been carried out or are being carried out.

These are:

1. The Programme for the development of renewable energies and energy efficiency (PRODERE).

This programme, amounting to 2,250,000,000 CFA francs, was conducted with the Company for Biofuels and Renewable Energies (SABER), based in Lome, in February 2014.

This project, executed by the company ASEMI, made it possible to install and make operational:

- 730 solar street lamps for public lighting in the towns of Cotonou, Parakou, Porto-Novo, Ketou, Porga, Tchaourou, Toucountouna and the universities of Abomey-Calavi and Parakou
- Six (06) solar mini-power plants installed in the localities of Tandou, Kabo (in the commune of Tchaourou), Oke Owo (in the commune of Save), Kpokissa (in the commune of Zogbodomey), Tchatingou and Toral & 2 (in the commune of Tanguieta). These installations are coupled with the village water supply system (AEV) for supplying drinking water to the beneficiary populations
- 164 individual kits installed to supply electric power to socio-community infrastructure
- 1,303 low-consumption lamps introduced in public lighting in the towns of Cotonou and Abomey-Calavi.

To date the project is fully completed and handed over. The pre-qualification procedure for companies to manage (lease) the micro-power plants is under way under the responsibility of SABER.

It should be noted that all the operations of tender studies and selection of bids as well as the payment of service providers were conducted by SABER.

The documents relating to each of these aspects have been deposited by SABER with the PRODERE focal point at the ministry in charge of Energy.

2. The Project for the installation of solar photovoltaic street lamps and kits (P1LaKS - PV), known as the American Project

This project, with a total cost of 4,135,488,180 CFA francs, financed from the national budget and executed by the company SUMEC-SOLEKTRA, made it possible to install:

- 1,500 solar street lamps spread over the whole national territory,
- 2,000 household kits in villages isolated from the national network such as Avlo, the millennium villages of Banikoara and Bonou and the border villages recently recovered from Nigeria following the border re-demarcation works,
- 200 kits of 1,000 Watts, used to supply electric power to health and security infrastructure.

3. The Solar Energy Development Project (PROVES)

This programme, with a total cost of 50 billion CFA francs, comprises two major components:

3.1 Solar street lamps component

For a total cost of 20 billion CFA francs, it made it possible to install, in an equitable manner, 15,000 solar street lamps in the 77 communes of our country.

3.2 Solar micro-power plants component

With a total cost of 30 billion, this component of the project is dedicated to:

- the construction of a low-voltage network varying between two and three kilometres depending on the locality, supplied by a solar field with a capacity of between 30 and 50 kWp depending on the locality.
- the construction of a water supply system with the construction of a 20 m3 water tower per locality,
- the provision of 100 meters per locality,
- the installation of 10 solar street lamps per locality for public lighting;

It is distributed as follows:

- lot 1 (ZTE): department of the Atlantique: 10 localities,
- lot 2 (ZTE): department of the Oueme-Plateau: 13 localities,
- lot 3 (AGETUR): department of the Mono-Couffo: 14 localities,
- lot 4 (SYSCOM): department of the Zou: 11 localities,
- lot 5 (ASEMI): department of the Zou-Collines: 15 localities,
- lot 6 (ASEMI): department of the Atacora: 15 localities,
- lot 7 (YANDALUX-MAYARICK): department of the Borgou: 13 localities,
- lot 8 (OTAMARI-AFRICA ENERGY): department of the Alibori: 15 localities.

IV - In the field of the SDGs-MDGs and major public works, since its creation the ministry in charge of the sector has worked for:

1. In respect of the MDGs-SDGs

It emerges from the evaluation of the MDGs in Benin, which is being finalised, that overall the following results have been obtained:

i. The enrolment rates, the girl-boy parity rate and the primary completion rate show a very good dynamic.

As regards the sphere of health, which on its own mobilises three MDGs, remarkable progress has been made in all the targets. This progress is most marked in the areas linked to accessibility to reproductive and procreative health care. Progress remains insufficient in terms of infant and maternal mortality and family contraception.

In the field of the living environment, the attainment of the target linked to accessibility to drinking water should be welcomed, as should the remarkable progress achieved at the African level in basic sanitation.

iv. As regards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), a National Strategy document for the Operationalisation of the SDGs (SNOODD) is being drawn up.

2. In respect of Major Public Works

- A master plan has been drawn up and adopted in the Council of Ministers and includes, among other things, the five flagship projects submitted to the Paris round table, namely:
  - Backbone (Epine Dorsale);
  - Programme for the construction of energy infrastructure and for the restructuring and extension of the energy distribution network;
  - Tourism development project for the fishermen's road (PDTRP);
  - Programme for the development of hydro-agricultural schemes in Benin;
  - Project to build a hospital of excellence.

3. In respect of the fulfilment of the commitments of the Paris round table

Establishment, with UNDP, of the Office for the operationalisation and monitoring of the round table (BOS-TR).

As at 31 December 2015, a total of 2,815.87 billion CFA francs, that is more than 46.5% of the financial partners' commitments at the round table, had been mobilised.

Drawing up of various documents by the BOS-TR, namely:

Establishment of a virtual information portal on the country's opportunities and developments for the benefit of the Diaspora.

4. In respect of the acceleration of reforms on the business climate and doing business

The main reforms implemented aim to:

- reduce the costs of setting up companies from 57,000 to 17,000 CFA francs;
- reduce the time needed to set up an establishment or a limited liability company (SARL) to 1 hour;
- continue promoting the support structures for business creation, in particular:
  - the One-stop shop for the formalisation of enterprises (GUFE),
  - the Business promotion centres (BPC),
  - the Approved management centres (CGA), or again the National Fund for the promotion of Enterprise and Youth Employment (FNPEEJ),
  - the National Microfinance Fund (FNM) and
  - the National Fund for Agricultural Development (FNDA), for the question relating to the financing of their agricultural, craft or tourism activities.

Results

- Benin, cited as the 2nd best "reformer" in the world, after Tajikistan, has not only recorded the strongest progression in this year's ranking among the 189 countries assessed, but has also progressed since 2012 from 175th place (out of 185) to 151st place (out of 189) today;
- Benin, 26th (out of 53) in Africa, thus achieves the 5th performance (out of 17) in the area of the Organisation for the Harmonisation of Business Law in Africa (OHADA);
- the business climate has clearly improved in Benin, according to the 2015 report, in a good number of areas.

Overall, the living conditions of the population have clearly improved; thus the non-monetary poverty rate fell from 44.3% in 2006 to 29.1% in 2011.

In the field of health, the overall review of the major achievements of the health sector reveals that from 2006 to 2015 the health sector benefited from investments of about 36 billion for health infrastructure and 40 billion for medico-technical equipment. These are investments made for the various projects of construction and equipment.

of hospitals financed by the national budget and by the technical and financial partners throughout the territory.

In terms of prospects, the following may be cited:

- The project to build and equip the zone hospital of Allada, whose source of financing is our partner Japan, for a grant of ten billion CFA francs;
- The project to build and equip the zone hospital of Save, whose technical and architectural studies are completely finished. It is financed by the Saudi fund up to 70% and by the national budget up to 30%;
- The project to build and equip the zone hospital of Tchaourou and six surrounding health centres, financed by the Kuwaiti Fund for about twelve billion CFA francs. The start of works will take place in the course of December 2016;
- The project to build and rehabilitate health facilities in Benin with financing from the BAIDC for nearly six billion CFA francs intended to improve the health equipment level (acquisition of MRI and various equipment). The technical studies are completed and the launch of tenders is under way;
- The project to build and equip the Mother and Child Hospital of Porto-Novo (HOMEP).

VI - In the field of agriculture, livestock and fisheries

One of the flagship reforms at the institutional level that marked the agricultural sector during the period under review is the drawing up and operationalisation of the Strategic Plan for the Revival of the Agricultural Sector (PSRSA). The overall objective is to improve the performance of Beninese agriculture, so as to make it capable of sustainably ensuring the food sovereignty of the population and of contributing to the economic and social development of Benin, to the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and to the reduction of poverty.

The PSRSA is based on nine strategies which concern inputs, mechanisation, financing, land development schemes, the professionalisation of farms, access to markets and to land, and the promotion of large farms. The institutional framework, one of whose main structures is the National Council for Orientation and Monitoring (CNOS) of the implementation of the PSRSA, has been set up.

Several other structures to support the operationalisation of actions in the agricultural sector have come into being on the government's initiative. These include the National Fund for Agricultural Development (FNDA), the Central Purchasing Body for Agricultural Inputs (CAIA), the Central Laboratory for Food Safety (LCSSA) and the Agency for the promotion of hydro-agricultural schemes (APAH).

1. Results obtained

1.1. Financing of the agricultural sector.

The budget of the agricultural sector rose from 39.8 billion in 2006 to 122.9 billion in 2014.

The threshold of 10% of the national budget recommended by the conference of African heads of State in Maputo in 2003 is thus exceeded. Expenditure in the agricultural sector comes to barely 7% on average per year of the whole general State budget.

Evolution of agricultural production over the period 2006-2014.

The main cash crops monitored recorded satisfactory growth rates. For example, cotton production increased by 63.47%, and that of pineapple more than tripled. Cereal production increased by 37.90%; that of roots and tubers recorded an increase of 63.47% and that of market gardening 83.4%.

As regards animal production, the monitoring of the three value chains selected in the PSRSA made it possible to observe that meat production recorded an increase of 25.18%; that of eggs an increase of 66.06%; and that of milk an increase of 22.74%.

Effects and impacts of the implementation of the reforms

On the economy. The growth rate of agricultural GDP rose from 5.6% in 2006 to 6.5% in 2015, with the particularity that it varied around 6.2% over the last four years. For its results Benin was rewarded by the FAO with two prizes in the field of nutritional and food security. It should also be noted that the field of agriculture constitutes an enormous reservoir of employment for young people, which needs to be explored further.

Prospects

By way of prospects, the following may be mentioned:

- The removal of the constraints linked to the perverse effects of climate change;
- The control of water;
- The commissioning and operation of the six agricultural product processing plants;
- The improvement of agricultural productivity;
- The effective implementation of the zoning of the cotton basin;
- The operationalisation of the agencies.

VII - In the sector of communication and information and communication technologies

A. Telecommunications, ICT (electronic communications) and postal sub-sector

In 2006, the ITU's recommendation for the transition from analogue to digital from 2015 onwards is an opportunity for the modernisation of broadcasting in Benin.

Results obtained

A - Telecommunications, ICT (electronic communications) and postal sub-sector

From April 2006 to March 2016, a significant evolution was observed in this sub-sector thanks to the strengthening of the legal and institutional framework of the sector, notably the passing of the law on electronic communications and on the post, which made possible an increase in the number of subscribers and an improvement in State revenue. The number of telephone subscribers (mobile and fixed) thus rose from 968,163 in 2006 to about 10,000,000 in 2016.

The landing of the second ACE submarine fibre-optic cable, the drawing up of the national frequency allocation plan, the creation and commissioning of the national centre for the control and management of the radio frequency spectrum at Hevie (Abomey-Calavi) and the drawing up of a national strategy for promoting high-speed internet are also tangible advances which have contributed appreciably to the current state of the sector.

Furthermore, the implementation of the project to develop telecommunications infrastructure in partnership with China should make it possible to increase the fibre-optic network in Benin from 1,000 to 3,000 km for the connection of all the commune capitals.

B. Information and communication sub-sector

The passing and promulgation of the law on the transition to digital terrestrial television, and the passing and promulgation of the law establishing the information and communication code. The programme to extend radio and television coverage made it possible to modernise the ORTB through the construction and equipping of 29 new transmitter centres, the creation of a second television channel BB 24, of a radio channel in national languages and of five regional stations. a1219.t:
The South Korean government provided €881,000 on Friday for humanitarian assistance in Cabo Delgado, in northern Mozambique, in the face of cyclones and armed attacks by rebel groups in the province since 2017.
“This contribution is dedicated to supporting the people of Mozambique, especially those affected by terrorism and natural disasters in Cabo Delgado,” said South Korea’s ambassador to Mozambique, Bok Won Kang, when announcing the fund in Maputo.
The fund of one million dollars (€881,000) will be used by the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) in Mozambique, in districts of Cabo Delgado affected by armed attacks since 2017, and should also benefit the victims of the last three cyclones that hit the country.
The fund should contribute to “long-term solutions” and will be used for food security, resilient infrastructure, combating malnutrition, hygiene, providing drinking water, health and protecting children in vulnerable situations, according to the IOM.
“The concrete intervention will be in infrastructure and actions based on the needs of the community and it was defined this way to create the greatest level of impact possible,” said the IOM’s shelter programme manager, Dinis Zacarias, during the announcement of the fund by South Korea.
The gas-rich province of Cabo Delgado has been facing an armed rebellion since 2017, which has caused thousands of deaths and a humanitarian crisis, with more than a million people displaced.
In 2024 alone, at least 349 people died in attacks by Islamic extremist groups in the province, an increase of 36% on the previous year, according to data recently released by the Africa Centre for Strategic Studies, an academic institution of the US Department of Defence that analyses conflicts in Africa.
Mozambique is at the end of the rainy season, which runs from October to April, a period in which, in addition to Jude, cyclones Chido, on 14 December, and Dikeledi, on 13 January, killed 313 people and left a trail of destruction.
Cyclone Jude, the most recent to affect the country, entered Mozambique through the Mossuril district and claimed at least 43 lives, 41 of them in Nampula. It also affected Tete, Manica, and Zambézia in the centre and Niassa and Cabo Delgado in the north.
On 27 March, the United Nations promised to advocate with Mozambique’s government to include funding for geospatial technologies in the state budget, as they are important for reducing the impact of natural disasters.
“We can advocate for United Nations member states to invest in these geospatial technologies (…), we have to continue to raise this issue at the political level so that the [Mozambique’s] government commits to funding through the State Budget,” said the United Nations resident coordinator in Mozambique, Catherine Sozi.
Mozambique is considered one of the territories most severely affected by global climate change. During the rainy season, it experiences cyclical floods and tropical cyclones, as well as prolonged periods of severe drought.
The United Nations has announced that it needs $222 million (€196 million) this year to assist around 1.4 million Mozambicans affected by the drought associated with the El Niño climate phenomenon, noting that only $41.5 million (€37 million) of this amount, corresponding to 19%, has been disbursed.

a1917.t:
- Britain's National Grid said it would pay customers to use less power, the first time it has used a new scheme to help prevent power outages.
- It would reward people via money off their bills for turning off appliances during a specific period when electricity demand is high.
- A separate measure calling on coal-fired power plants to fire up as back up power was stood down for Monday evening as the supply picture had improved.
Britain's National Grid said it would pay customers to use less power on Monday and Tuesday evenings this week, the first time it has used a new scheme designed to help prevent power shortages.
More than a million households and business are signed up to the Demand Flexibility Service (DFS), which rewards people, usually via money off their bills, for turning off appliances such as ovens and dishwashers during a specific period when electricity demand is high.
National Grid warned in October that homes could face three-hour rolling power cuts this winter if the country was unable to secure enough gas and electricity imports. It launched the DFS as part of its tool box to help prevent cuts.
The service, which has been trialled but not run in a live situation before, would run from 17:00 to 18:00 on Monday, it said, adding that the move did not mean electricity supplies were at risk and advised people not to worry.
The measures were announced in order to "ensure that everyone gets the electricity they need," Craig Dyke, head of national control at National Grid ESO, told BBC Radio on Monday, adding that 26 suppliers had signed up for the scheme.
Below-freezing temperatures have been recorded across much of the UK in recent days with the national weather service, the Met Office, last week issuing severe weather warnings for snow and ice.
A separate measure calling on coal-fired power plants to fire up as back up power was stood down for Monday evening as the supply picture had improved, a National Grid spokesperson told Reuters via telephone.
However, National Grid said three coal-fired plants had been instructed to warm up to be on standby for Tuesday, and also called on those signed up to the DFS programme to again curb electricity use between 16:30 and 18:00.
The National Grid's ESO said in a statement:
Jonathan Brearley, chief executive of British Energy regulator Ofgem, said on Monday the country's overall power supply outlook had improved from when National Grid first warned of potential power cuts.
He said high gas stocks in Europe and an improvement in the operation of French nuclear plants, which often provide electricity to Britain via several power links, had helped to ease the supply risks.
However, "as today's events show ... we need to remain vigilant and cautious about what may happen in the future," he said at an Institute of Government event.

a2039.t:
Alors près de 2000 Guinéens sont menacés d’expulsion des États-Unis, la Présidence de la République, par la voix de son ministre Porte-parole, a apporté une précision de taille quant à l’assistance du gouvernement guinéen à ces concitoyens en détresse. C’était lors de son passage ce vendredi 7 février 2025 dans l’émission ‘’On fait le point’’ de la Radiotélévision Guinéenne.
Le général Amara Camara a assuré que le président Mamadi Doumbouya est prêt « comme il l’a toujours fait », à porter secours en cas de nécessité.
« Nos concitoyens qui ont besoin de l’accompagnement partout où ils se trouvent, le président Mamadi Doumbouya est prêt à leur apporter de l’aide, comme il l’a toujours fait. Partout où les Guinéens se sentiront menacés et exprimeront le besoin d’être assistés par le Président, sa main tendue sera là » a-t-il assuré.
Le Secrétaire Général de la Présidence de la République a aussi soutenu que les relations entre les États-Unis et la Guinée sont au beau fixe. Il assure par ailleurs que la Guinée est disposée à travailler avec l’Administration américaine.
« Nous voulons réaffirmer ici et dire à tout le monde que la Guinée entretient d’excellentes relations avec les États-Unis. Ces relations, nous faisons en sorte de les réchauffer au mieux. Nous sommes disposés à travailler avec l’Administration américaine dans l’intérêt de nos pays respectifs », a-t-il annoncé.
a2039.en:
Guineans threatened with deportation from the United States: here is what the Presidency intends to do

With nearly 2,000 Guineans threatened with deportation from the United States, the Presidency of the Republic, through its spokesperson minister, provided an important clarification regarding the Guinean government's assistance to these compatriots in distress. This came during his appearance on Friday 7 February 2025 on the programme "On fait le point" on Guinean Radio and Television.

General Amara Camara assured that President Mamadi Doumbouya is ready, "as he has always done," to come to their aid should the need arise.

"Our compatriots who need support, wherever they are, President Mamadi Doumbouya is ready to bring them help, as he has always done. Wherever Guineans feel threatened and express the need to be assisted by the President, his outstretched hand will be there," he assured.

The Secretary General of the Presidency of the Republic also maintained that relations between the United States and Guinea are in excellent shape. He further assured that Guinea is prepared to work with the American Administration.

"We want to reaffirm here and tell everyone that Guinea maintains excellent relations with the United States. We are doing our utmost to warm these relations. We are prepared to work with the American Administration in the interest of our respective countries," he announced.

a2100.t:
Sean Jones assumed leadership of USAID Ethiopia in July of 2019. USAID Ethiopia is one of the largest USAID missions in Africa and is a focus country for presidential initiatives covering HIV and AIDS, malaria, child survival, agricultural growth, food security and nutrition, climate change and energy. The mission’s portfolio also has a robust basic education program and activities that promote good governance and prevent conflicts. 
Prior to this, Sean served as the Senior Deputy Assistant Administrator in USAID’s Bureau for Food Security, which leads the U.S. Government’s Feed the Future initiative. 
He talked to Capital about his future plan and how the mission supports the country’s fight against poverty. Excerpts; 
Capital: What are your plans during your stay?
Sean Jones: I believe USAID is here because we have things to offer. America wants friends and partners like Ethiopia. The best ideas, resources and some of our capacity to help Ethiopia through this historic period of time that Ethiopia needs right now.
Right now there are many reforms underway that are more focused on democratic values and systems, so our support will be helping Ethiopia in the upcoming election by supporting the election board, we also want to support substantially and the economic reform agenda of the government in line with American values we also need to support the people who need food assistance and humanitarian assistance and crisis response.
Capital: What are your plans in the healthcare sector? 
Sean Jones: There is a commitment to stop the spread of HIV. We also want to help alleviate tuberculosis and malaria, we want to continue that, we are not dramatically changing, our level of investment to maintain the gains that Ethiopia has made with HIV in particular, the cases have dropped substantially thanks to the tremendous support and commitment of the Ethiopian government to ensure that the case load is down and identifying new cases very quickly by working with the targeted populations.
Capital: What is the status of tuberculosis in the country currently?
Sean Jones: We signed a MOU to continue working with the Ministry of Health. The health system is sufficiently strong now so we are working with civil society organizations.
Capital: Can you tell us about the justice reform program called FITIH?
Sean Jones: This program helps protect the rights of citizens and updates the justice system. We are working with the Attorney General and the Ministry of Peace to strengthen the way that it engages with the public to review laws that may need updating and provide additional capacity for Ethiopia’s lawyers, judges and prosecutors. It has some focus on capacity building and how to technically implement Ethiopia’s vision.
Capital: How are you helping the electoral board?
Sean Jones: Outside of the National Electoral Board of Ethiopia (NEBE), we are helping civil society organizations and citizens to engage with NEBE to provide advice, on how to conduct free and fair elections.
Capital: Do you think the election will be conducted on the scheduled time?
Sean Jones: It is the government’s decision but we want to ensure NEBE is as strong as possible for the election. It is a lot of organization, a lot of people, a lot of things have to happen. NEBE is one part of that. The other is the government ensuring security.
Capital: You work with private sector. Can you tell us about the meat processing plant in Jigjiga.
Sean Jones: I just have had the opportunity to talk with the general manager, owner and founder of the factory, he closed it temporarily and wants to have another project in that area to grow food for the livestock. Actually he is increasing investment in that area so that he can have a long consistent supply for the factory, that is a tremendous support for the country and I am proud of the investors working in that region investing substantial money. More broadly our investment in the private sector is very important like now, we have had private sector involvement for a long time but it hasn’t been strong necessarily as it could be. A robust private sector will do wonders for economic growth.
Capital: How are you actually helping the private sector?
Sean Jones: In policy we are working with government officials on reforms to help the private sector. We are working to help businesspeople and farmers to access finance, we are also working with financial institutions so business can access land and resources.
Capital: How are you involved in the Agricultural sector?
Sean Jones: We want to help Ethiopia have less reliance on external factors to grow, produce and sell food while making sure that the crops are healthy.
Capital: What is your take on hybrid seeds? 
Sean Jones: The US government basis this on the needs of the country, not every country desires hybrid seeds, not every country needs genetically modified seeds. Our programs works in this manner, especially in Ethiopia to try and understand what Ethiopia really needs and provide that assistance, experience across the world. We are mobilizing that experience.
As related to hybrid or other types of seed technology we do believe that every country should make their own decisions regarding what types of seeds and technologies and approaches they want to bring to their local market.
Capital: So how are you helping the farmers boost their products?
Sean Jones: One is seed varieties. This could be local seeds, weather controlling pests and other pests’ like fungus, or it could be the introduction of hybrid seeds that are outside of Ethiopia we work with as well, and when Ethiopia’s ready, in a position to have genetically produced seeds or other types of seed technologies we support that, we are not pushing to do that right now we want to have Ethiopian farmers help to have access to seed varieties.
Capital: You help set up some seed shops, and these shops are selling only your own products that came from you directly. Does USAID fund them?
Sean Jones: So that is not accurate. I appreciate that because I can help correct it, we went into partnership with a company called Dow DuPont which changed their name to Corteva, what we did is we introduced tens of thousands of farmers to new products that were legally brought by this company and also other companies. We didn’t fund them, this is done by the private sector, we encouraged them to use better products. 
Capital: Isn’t it possible they will become dependent on certain fertilizers? 
Sean Jones: That is true in general not specific to Corteva, if seed technology has patent rights, and a lot of seed technology doesn’t germinate every year, that is true. I think that is farmers’ decision whether they can continue or use local seeds even hybrid varieties where they do germinate every year. They can see higher production yield and a higher rate of protection in their farming.
Capital: What are you doing to help Ethiopia with its economic reform? 
Sean Jones: This is a new area in our assistance program in Ethiopia, again we are really proud to be invited to provide assistance to the Ministry of Finance, the Prime Minster and the Central Bank. We have brought in a very famous economist and signed a three-year contract and his team from Harvard University to provide advice to the very capable people here the Ethiopian people are leading this reform effort they came and provide assessment, and diagnostics. Particularly it is a critical period for Ethiopia and Ethiopia’s economy.
Capital: How can we be sure about their advice? 
Sean Jones: They didn’t come and start offering advice for them; there are also a bunch of Ethiopian teams that travel here and back to Harvard University in the US. They give advice considering global perspectives, and bring some of the best ideas. It is a conversation between really brilliant people there in Addis Ababa leading reforms and people from Harvard.
Capital: Is there anything you want to add?
Sean Jones: We have a lot of projects focused on helping the Ethiopian people one thing about USAID is that we are invited here and we are proud to be a partner of the people and government.

a2357.t:
The US government has abruptly terminated aid to South African organisations providing critical support for HIV and AIDS, leaving many programmes in jeopardy.
Recipients of funding under the US government’s President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS (PEPFAR) received notification overnight that their grants have been permanently ended.
In the correspondence seen by APA, the US Agency for International Development (USAID) said the termination was done in the “interest of the US government.”
“This award is being terminated for convenience and the interests of the U.S. Government pursuant to a directive from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in his capacity as the Acting Administrator for the US Agency for International Development,” the letter said.
It further explained that the decision stemmed from an assessment that continuing these programmes did not align with US national interests.
Recipients were directed to immediately halt all activities related to their awards and inform any subrecipients or contractors accordingly.
The sudden withdrawal of support raises concerns over the future of vital healthcare services addressing one of South Africa’s most pressing public health challenges.
Since its inception in 2003, PEPFAR has allocated approximately $8 billion to combat the HIV epidemic in South Africa, one of the countries with high infection rates.
For the current fiscal year alone, running from October 2024 to September 2025, about $439 million was earmarked for these efforts in the country.
In addition to PEPFAR-funded initiatives, USAID-supported district health projects not directly linked to PEPFAR are also being instructed to cease operations.
JN/APA

a2363.t:
Le gouvernement botswanais prévoit de relocaliser plus de 400 demandeurs d’asile déboutés actuellement détenus au Centre pour immigrants illégaux de Francistown vers le camp de réfugiés de Dukwi. Cette décision intervient à la suite de critiques croissantes concernant les violations des droits humains liées à leur détention prolongée.
Le ministre de la Justice et des Services pénitentiaires, Nelson Ramaotwana, a annoncé pour bientôt le relogement des refoulés, lors d’une visite sur les sites de Francistown et de Dukwi. Il a souligné qu’il s’inscrivait dans une politique gouvernementale axée sur le respect de la dignité humaine, conformément aux engagements du président Duma Boko.
« Le terme Centre pour immigrants illégaux laisse penser à un lieu de transit, mais il s’agit en réalité d’une prison », a déclaré le ministre, déplorant également la séparation systématique des familles dans le centre.
Il a expliqué que les enfants sont souvent séparés de leurs mères ou de leurs pères, et placés sous la garde d’adultes sans lien familial.
« Les garçons sans père sont confiés à des hommes étrangers, et les filles à des femmes qui ne sont pas de leur famille », a-t-il précisé.
Dans ce contexte, le gouvernement a pris la décision de libérer ces demandeurs d’asile et de les transférer vers le camp de Dukwi, où ils bénéficieront de meilleures conditions de vie et d’un meilleur accès à l’aide humanitaire.
Depuis plusieurs années, le Botswana encourage le rapatriement volontaire des réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile vers leurs pays d’origine. Toutefois, de nombreux concernés refusent ce retour, invoquant l’insécurité et l’instabilité persistantes dans leurs pays.
La politique actuelle de détention prolongée a suscité l’indignation d’organisations de défense des droits humains, qui dénoncent le traitement carcéral réservé à des personnes en situation de vulnérabilité.
Le processus de relocalisation devrait s’échelonner sur deux à quatre semaines.
JN/fss/te/Sf/APA
a2363.en:
The Botswana government plans to relocate more than 400 rejected asylum seekers currently held at the Centre for Illegal Immigrants in Francistown to the Dukwi refugee camp. This decision comes following growing criticism concerning human rights violations linked to their prolonged detention.

The Minister of Justice and Prison Services, Nelson Ramaotwana, announced that the rehousing of those turned away would take place soon, during a visit to the Francistown and Dukwi sites. He stressed that it was part of a government policy focused on respect for human dignity, in line with the commitments of President Duma Boko.

"The term Centre for Illegal Immigrants suggests a place of transit, but it is in reality a prison," the minister declared, also deploring the systematic separation of families in the centre.

He explained that children are often separated from their mothers or their fathers, and placed in the care of adults with no family ties to them.

"Boys without fathers are entrusted to strange men, and girls to women who are not their family," he specified.

In this context, the government has taken the decision to release these asylum seekers and to transfer them to the Dukwi camp, where they will benefit from better living conditions and better access to humanitarian aid.

For several years, Botswana has encouraged the voluntary repatriation of refugees and asylum seekers to their countries of origin. However, many of those concerned refuse this return, citing the persistent insecurity and instability in their countries.

The current policy of prolonged detention has provoked the indignation of human rights organisations, which denounce the prison-like treatment reserved for people in a vulnerable situation.

The relocation process should be spread over two to four weeks.

JN/fss/te/Sf/APA

a2457.t:
According to Ministry of Health spokesperson Christopher Nyanga, following their initial statement that the United States of America (USA) will withdraw from the World Health Organization, which would not affect the availability of ARVs, the ministry has now confirmed the cessation of operations at a few agencies. “There are multiple civil society organisations and non-governmental organisations operating in the health space that were directly affected by the decision to suspend support,” Nyanga said.
He added that following this decision most CSOs and NGOs, especially arms performing functions in the HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment, have since closed for business like Tebelopele Voluntary Testing and Counselling centres across the country, "in compliance with the decision”. The ministry has since then advised Batswana to opt for public health services as there is uncertainty as to how long this predicament will persist. Nyanga assured citizens that despite the recent developments, government would still be able to meet the demands of such services. “The ministry also wishes to inform the public that all possible efforts will be made to avail lubricants, condoms and other preventive devices at both public and private facilities so that no gap is experienced,” MoH communicated. The ministry highlighted that to mitigate the situation it would ensure that there are ARVs available at post offices despite the discontinued services at the centres. The latest developments are marked by the return of Trump who has now ceased most of US funding to global agencies, USAID and WHO.
“Safety first is safety always”– Charles M HayesAs most people begin travelling across the country to spend the President’s Holidays with family and friends, there is every reason to embrace the joy and togetherness that this period brings.While holiday periods bring joy, they are sadly often accompanied by a rise in road accidents, violent incidents and other avoidable tragedies. Too often, families that set out to celebrate together end...

a2735.t:
O Relatório Económico sobre África (ERA) 2025, publicado pela Comissão Económica das Nações Unidas para África (ECA), destaca a necessidade urgente de impulsionar a resiliência económica do continente. Segundo o documento, o crescimento económico africano deverá recuperar gradualmente para 3,8% em 2025 e 4,1% em 2026, impulsionado pelo aumento do consumo privado e pela melhoria do comércio.
No entanto, o relatório alerta que este crescimento ainda está abaixo do necessário para melhorar significativamente os padrões de vida e alcançar os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS). Além disso, a economia africana enfrenta riscos significativos, incluindo tensões globais, conflitos regionais e choques climáticos mais frequentes e severos.
Dívida e desafios económicos
Apesar de uma redução no rácio dívida/PIB de 67,3% em 2023 para 62,1% em 2025, os níveis de endividamento continuam elevados, dificultando investimentos essenciais para o desenvolvimento. O relatório destaca a necessidade de reformar a arquitetura financeira global, uma vez que os custos elevados de empréstimos limitam o crescimento económico da região.
Embora a taxa de pobreza extrema em África esteja a diminuir, o número total de pessoas em situação de pobreza aumentou para 468 milhões, agravado por crises recentes. Além disso, a falta de oportunidades para os 76 milhões de jovens africanos sem emprego, educação ou formação representa um desafio crítico. O relatório enfatiza que investir no desenvolvimento de competências é essencial para o crescimento sustentável do continente.
Mudanças climáticas e comércio intra-africano
O documento também alerta para os impactos das mudanças climáticas, que afetaram mais de 110 milhões de pessoas em 2022 e causaram perdas econômicas superiores a 8,5 mil milhões de dólares. Diante desse cenário, a ECA recomenda que os países africanos acelerem ações climáticas para fortalecer a resiliência econômica.
O relatório aponta a Área de Comércio Livre Continental Africana (AFCFTA) como um fator-chave para reduzir a dependência externa e fortalecer a autossuficiência e o comércio intrarregional. Com a crescente instabilidade das relações comerciais globais, a AFCFTA pode oferecer novas oportunidades para o crescimento sustentável do continente.
Sobre a ECA
Criada em 1958 pelo Conselho Económico e Social das Nações Unidas (ECOSOC), a Comissão Económica das Nações Unidas para África (ECA) visa promover o desenvolvimento económico e social no continente, fomentar a integração regional e incentivar a cooperação internacional. A organização conta com 54 Estados-membros e desempenha um papel estratégico no cenário institucional africano.
Adelise Furtado
*Estagiária
a2735.en:
Economic Report on Africa warns of the challenges of resilience

The Economic Report on Africa (ERA) 2025, published by the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA), highlights the urgent need to boost the continent’s economic resilience. According to the document, African economic growth should gradually recover to 3.8% in 2025 and 4.1% in 2026, driven by increased private consumption and improved trade.

However, the report warns that this growth is still below what is needed to significantly improve living standards and to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In addition, the African economy faces significant risks, including global tensions, regional conflicts and more frequent and severe climate shocks.

Debt and economic challenges

Despite a reduction in the debt-to-GDP ratio from 67.3% in 2023 to 62.1% in 2025, debt levels remain high, hampering investments that are essential for development. The report highlights the need to reform the global financial architecture, since high borrowing costs limit the region’s economic growth.

Although the extreme poverty rate in Africa is falling, the total number of people living in poverty has risen to 468 million, aggravated by recent crises. In addition, the lack of opportunities for the 76 million African young people without employment, education or training represents a critical challenge. The report emphasises that investing in skills development is essential for the continent’s sustainable growth.

Climate change and intra-African trade

The document also warns of the impacts of climate change, which affected more than 110 million people in 2022 and caused economic losses of more than 8.5 billion dollars. Faced with this scenario, the ECA recommends that African countries accelerate climate action in order to strengthen economic resilience.

The report points to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a key factor in reducing external dependence and strengthening self-sufficiency and intra-regional trade. With the growing instability of global trade relations, the AfCFTA may offer new opportunities for the continent’s sustainable growth.

About the ECA

Created in 1958 by the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) aims to promote economic and social development on the continent, foster regional integration and encourage international cooperation. The organisation has 54 member States and plays a strategic role in the African institutional landscape.

Adelise Furtado
*Intern

a2809.t:
By: Fistum Getachew
Population data show that Ethiopia is a country of more than 130 million people, of whom more than 70% are youths below the age of thirty. This demographic profile is true of many countries in Africa. Similarly, statistics show that Ethiopia is also one of the biggest economies in Africa and a country that is growing fast. In the past ten to fifteen years alone, it has been steadily growing at one of the fastest rates, despite the many challenges it had to overcome. There were issues of security and peace in some pockets of the country. In particular, there was the conflict in the north that lasted two years, and the COVID pandemic, which has left its negative mark even on developed countries, let alone those which are poor and without adequate medical facilities and infrastructure. But Ethiopia managed to cope with it, pushing aside all the negative predictions forwarded against it.
All these features tell us that Ethiopia’s march toward a bigger and stronger economy is relentless and unstoppable, and this has been confirmed and testified by academics and researchers in politics and economics, including international financial institutions and think tanks. Ethiopia’s role in the diplomatic world of Africa and more generally in the world has also been growing, owing to its very important geopolitical position in the Horn of Africa.
Besides, Ethiopia’s long and glorious history also makes it an important nation in Africa with its influence. If it has been admitted to the BRICS body, it is not by chance but because it has deserved it. What is more, its contribution to peacekeeping and peacemaking both in Africa as well as in more distant countries, in collaboration and under the auspices of international organizations such as the UN, the AU, and IGAD, has earned it a huge reputation and a relatively notable clout in international affairs.
History tells us that Ethiopia has never been without access to the sea, except during the past thirty years when there were sudden and unexpected developments with the cessation of Eritrea from Ethiopia. If we look deeply at Ethiopia’s long history, it has always had access to the sea with its own ports, but also had a sizeable maritime force with a fleet of its own ships that facilitated its engagement in trade and commerce with the rest of the world.
Today, it is sad to see that it is without access to the sea. This fact has made it a prisoner and isolated in a world of abundance. In fact, it is the only country in the world that is landlocked with such a big population and is so near to the sea, with only some kilometers away.
According to international law, any country which needs access to the sea has the right to seek and obtain it based on international law and practice, with an arrangement of some type with adjacent countries to the sea. It can seek access to the sea based on the principle of "give and take" in a peaceful and diplomatic manner. We have seen such arrangements in many countries. It is a principle that the entire world practices, and there would be no scandal if Ethiopia as well proposed this idea to its neighbors. Clearly, it would be a win-win stance aimed at more integration, not only in economic terms but also in political, diplomatic, cultural, and people-to-people relations.
Economists say that a country without access to the sea would see its economic growth constrained by up to forty percent, which is staggering. Ethiopia cannot afford to limit its growth because it has an expanding population and a growing economy. It definitely needs access to the sea because its economy depends strongly on its continuous and unhindered exchange of trade with other countries. It exports products to the international market to secure the foreign currency it needs to import the materials it needs for its economic progress. It needs to import technological equipment, fertilizers, vehicles, and other products that are not available in the country, such as pharmaceutical and other medical appliances. Hence, access to the sea for Ethiopia is practically an existential issue.
Economists have also noted that if Ethiopia does not have access to the sea, there will be many and unpredictable repercussions, including potentially dangerous scenarios. A population that is growing at the current pace will produce so many people who need employment opportunities, and if the economy does not grow at a pace that accommodates the needs of the country, there would be an explosion of hopeless youths, and this could give birth to many repercussions, including dangers to the security and stability of the country. Unemployed youths are very often susceptible to being recruited for criminal purposes such as terrorism, human trafficking, and even drug trafficking.
There could be the need for these millions of youths to try and emigrate, taking dangerous routes with the complicity of human traffickers. We have seen uncountable times how many have perished in the deserts and how many in the sea, traveling in dangerous and overloaded dinghies. We have noted thousands who have drowned while trying to cross to Europe or the Middle East in search of jobs and economic viability.
We know that a huge crisis is still underway on an international level and the developed countries are trying to cope with this issue by supporting the economies of those countries from where many migrants come, and adding more on that or sabotaging these efforts would be counterproductive. That is also why landlocked countries which cannot have access to the sea are allowed to seek and obtain some sort of arrangement and need to be given the opportunity to grow and prevent such dangerous exodus that has a huge impact even in the advanced economies.
The Horn of Africa is one of the regions that produce many migrants, and the main source of such a crisis is mainly economic, besides certain peace and security issues. Even the political crises of many countries that result in hostilities and conflicts have their origin in economic shortfalls. No one would engage in migration if there were comfortable conditions at home, and the first cause of migration is hence extreme poverty and deprivation.
Ethiopia does not want to contribute to such a crisis, and the only solution is to access the sea and create the conditions for more engagement in more development and progress to liberate its citizens from want and despair. If Ethiopia grows, it could also contribute to the growth of its neighbors because economic integration facilitates more growth, more exchange of commerce and trade, and more prosperity. In reality, the fact that Ethiopia has now built the largest dam in Africa in GERD (the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile) can be viewed as one of the factors that would enhance economic integration because neighbors of Ethiopia would have access to cheap and clean energy.
Ethiopia’s current trajectory of growth absolutely needs more outlets to the sea and not to rely on only one or two ports. That is why many say that access to the sea for Ethiopia is a matter of "to be or not to be!" Anyway, Ethiopia is confident that it will find a way to secure access to the sea sooner rather than later because it would also benefit the country that agrees to grant it such access to the sea. The mentality of a zero-sum game should be fought not to keep all our peoples in perennial poverty.

a2960.t:
- Nigerian lawmakers probe over a dozen non-profits' finances and funding sources over the past decade.
- The investigation targets groups involved in human rights work, some previously funded by USAID.
- Critics claim the probe is an attempt to undermine non-profits and clamp down on free speech.
Nigerian lawmakers are probing the activities of more than a dozen non-profit organisations and demanded they submit tax and financial statements dating back a decade within a week, a letter seen by Reuters showed, prompting accusations of "bullying".
The groups affected include some previously funded by the US Agency for International Development (USAID), Washington's primary humanitarian aid agency whose work has been largely frozen by the Trump administration for 90 days pending assessments of their effectiveness.
A committee of Nigeria's House of Representatives sent letters to groups involved in human rights and accountability work, including Transparency International Nigeria, informing them of the probe "with a view to unravelling their real identities, sources of funding and what they expend their monies on".
The letter said the investigation was a response to comments made last month by US Congressman Scott Perry, who, without providing evidence, said USAID had funnelled money to various Islamist groups worldwide, including Boko Haram in Nigeria.
Richard Mills, the US ambassador to Nigeria, rejected Perry's assertion regarding Boko Haram.
Nigerian lawmakers are demanding audited statements from civil society groups, their funding sources, and how they spent their money between 2015 and 2024.
Some of the groups said the investigation was an excuse to undermine their work and amounted to a clampdown on free speech.
"On the basis of hearsay, just an unfounded allegation and lack of any proven evidence from either Nigerian security or Nigerian financial agencies, the national assembly will embark on this walk," Auwal Musa Rafsanjani, head of Transparency International in Nigeria, told Reuters.
Abiodun Baiyewu, the executive director of Global Rights, which is also being investigated, said of the investigation: "It is a brazen attempt at bullying the non-profit sector and not done in good faith."
A House of Representatives spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment on the matter.
Parliamentary committees in Nigeria can investigate any issue deemed of national interest, and their reports, if adopted by a majority of lawmakers, can lead to the arrest or prosecution of groups or people.

a3558.t:
Na hora do fecho deste artigo – pouco passa das 3h da manhã em Cabo Verde, ainda não há certezas sobre quem será o próximo inquilino na Casa Branca, nuns Estados-cada-vez-mais-desunidos-da-América. Segundo o modelo eleitoral do New York Times, a hipótese de vitória está mais inclinada para Donald Trump.
Também em destaque está a reportagem sobre o roubo de gado em Santiago.
O roubo de animais é considerado uma “praga” pelos criadores rurais, que enfrentam uma realidade angustiante porque dependente de cada cabeça de gado para o seu sustento. O cenário de insegurança e ameaça de ladrões tem afectado o quotidiano de quem vive da criação de animais, especialmente nas áreas mais afastadas onde o apoio é mínimo e a esperança quase inexistente.
Na capa desta edição também abordamos a abertura de mais um ano judicial.
Na tradicional Sessão Solene de Abertura do Ano Judicial, realizada esta terça-feira, os principais representantes da Justiça reafirmaram o seu compromisso com esta dimensão fundamental da sociedade e da democracia. Num sistema que procura modernização e aperfeiçoamento em meio de vários desafios crónicos, foram reconhecidos avanços significativos. Contudo, os discursos proferidos destacam também a necessidade de investimentos robustos; a urgência em tornar o sector mais ágil, bem como a ideia de que a Justiça é uma responsabilidade colectiva que deve ser acompanhada por uma “cultura de resultados”.
A questão do tráfico de drogas sintéticas em Cabo Verde é, também, tema em destaque nesta edição do Expresso das Ilhas.
A recente detenção de um homem de 35 anos na posse de 72,33 grama de MDMA (ecstasy), em Tira-Chapéu, na Praia, volta a levantar a preocupação da circulação deste tipo de estupefacientes em Cabo Verde.
A destacar igualmente a edição deste ano da Ocean Week que decorre em São Vicente.
Na abertura da Ocean Week, Correia e Silva colocou oceano no centro do desenvolvimento nacional.
A ler, também, o artigo de opinião ‘Orçamento do Estado 2025: Um marco para a inclusão, crescimento e equidade em Cabo Verde’ da autoria de Luís Carlos Silva
a3558.en:
As this article goes to press – it is just past 3 a.m. in Cabo Verde – there is still no certainty about who will be the next tenant in the White House, in an ever-more-disunited United States of America. According to the New York Times’ electoral model, the probability of victory leans more towards Donald Trump.

Also featured is the report on cattle theft in Santiago.

The theft of animals is considered a “plague” by rural breeders, who face a distressing reality because they depend on every head of cattle for their livelihood. The climate of insecurity and the threat of thieves has affected the daily life of those who live from animal husbandry, especially in the most remote areas where support is minimal and hope almost non-existent.

On the cover of this edition we also address the opening of another judicial year.

At the traditional Solemn Session for the Opening of the Judicial Year, held this Tuesday, the main representatives of the Justice system reaffirmed their commitment to this fundamental dimension of society and of democracy. In a system seeking modernisation and improvement amid several chronic challenges, significant advances were acknowledged. However, the speeches delivered also highlight the need for robust investment; the urgency of making the sector more agile, as well as the idea that Justice is a collective responsibility that must be accompanied by a “culture of results”.

The question of synthetic drug trafficking in Cabo Verde is also a featured topic in this edition of Expresso das Ilhas.

The recent arrest of a 35-year-old man in possession of 72.33 grams of MDMA (ecstasy), in Tira-Chapéu, Praia, again raises concern about the circulation of this type of narcotic in Cabo Verde.

Also to be highlighted is this year’s edition of Ocean Week, taking place in São Vicente.

At the opening of Ocean Week, Correia e Silva placed the ocean at the centre of national development.

Also worth reading is the opinion article ‘State Budget 2025: A milestone for inclusion, growth and equity in Cabo Verde’ by Luís Carlos Silva.

a3616.t:
Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, has called for a new vision for global health that places Africa at the core of future governance, trade, financing and innovation.
Speaking on Tuesday at the Africa Health Sovereignty Summit in Accra, Ghana, Mr Pate challenged existing frameworks that reduced global health to a narrow set of diseases or priorities largely shaped by external narratives:
He said global health is often described through the lens of a few priority issues, like HIV, malaria and tuberculosis, or through specific areas such as health financing or maternal and child health.
“Yet these issues are framed by externally driven perspectives, leaving African voices, especially from poorer countries, less acknowledged,” he said.
The minister explained that most health progress in lower-income countries over the past 25 years has depended on domestic financing and local leadership, with donor support playing a complementary role.
He warned that shifting geopolitics and nationalist tendencies demand a recalibration.
“We cannot build healthier populations purely on the generosity of other nations. It is time to define our path, rooted in sovereignty and aligned with local needs,” he said.
He traced the evolution of global health to two contrasting legacies.
“The first is the positive legacy of 19th-century international sanitary cooperation, which laid the foundation for today’s collaborative institutions.
“The second is the colonial legacy, rooted in tropical medicine and neo-colonial economic structures, issues that were powerfully critiqued by Ghana’s Kwame Nkrumah,” he said.
He noted the continuity of structural inequities, despite efforts ranging from the Bandung Conference in 1955 and the Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978, to global debt initiatives and public health commissions.
He said donor-driven priorities routinely undermine national agency and compromise the independence of institutions like the WHO.
“Too often, macroeconomic metrics prioritise short-term ‘value for money’ over the critical public health investments our people need, such as sanitation, clean water, waste management and nutrition,” he said.
He warned of fragmentation and dwindling resources despite these structural flaws and the emergence of over 70 global health partnerships like the Global Fund, Gavi and CEPI.
To reclaim leadership in global health,” he said, “we must act decisively through a seven-point strategic framework.
Mr Pate said the region must forge a strategic South-South alliance, uniting Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean to form a new geopolitical axis that, while mindful of global power dynamics, remains committed to equity-driven governance.
He said it is also essential to revise trade terms restricting manufacturing capacity and limiting access to essential medicines.
He added that the continent must champion true country ownership and accountability.
“We must push for a more independent and effective WHO by restructuring its funding model to emphasise predictable, unearmarked contributions that allow for impartial and equitable leadership.
“We need to prioritise domestic financing models. This includes exploring innovative instruments such as pooled regional health funds, diaspora bonds, and blended finance approaches that reduce overreliance on foreign aid,” he said.
He said it is important to industrialise the health trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
“This means engaging trade and finance ministries to build infrastructure for continental markets, harmonise professional standards, and support the health value chain, from diagnostics and test kits to digital health platforms.
